name: Pawn structure
mnemonic: Pawns are the skeleton; pieces are the muscles. Attack a chain at its base.
summary: Pawns can't move backwards, so their placement decides which squares are strong, which are weak, and where each side should play.
points: A pawn chain (here d4–e5) is strongest at its head and weakest at its base: Black attacks d4 with ...c5 and the head with ...f6.
Pawns point to where you should attack: White's chain points to the kingside, Black's to the queenside.
Isolated, doubled and backward pawns are long-term weaknesses; passed pawns are long-term strengths.

practice.prompt: Click the base of White's pawn chain — the square Black should attack.
practice.explain: d4 is the base of the d4–e5 chain; ...c5 hits it.

name: Weak squares
mnemonic: A hole is a square no pawn can ever guard again.
summary: A square that can no longer be defended by a pawn is a permanent home for enemy pieces.
points: After ...e5 in the Najdorf, d5 can't be covered by a black pawn any more — it's a hole.
Black compensates by controlling d5 with pieces (...Be6, ...Nbd7–b6) or by forcing the ...d5 break.
Every pawn move creates a potential weakness behind it — move pawns with a purpose.

practice.prompt: Click the hole in Black's position.
practice.explain: After ...e5 no black pawn can ever control d5.

name: Outposts
mnemonic: A knight on an outpost is like a tooth in the opponent's jaw.
summary: An outpost is a square in enemy territory, protected by your pawn, that no enemy pawn can attack. Knights love them.
points: The d5-knight is supported by two pawns and can never be chased by a black pawn (no c- or e-pawn can reach c6/e6).
From d5 it hits c7, e7, b6 and f6 — it controls Black's whole position.
The only way to remove it is to trade a piece for it; often Black has no suitable piece.

practice.prompt: Click White's outpost square.
practice.explain: d5 is protected by White's pawns and can't be attacked by a black pawn.

name: Open files
mnemonic: Rooks belong on open files — and then on the 7th rank.
summary: A file with no pawns is a highway for rooks. Controlling it lets your rooks invade the enemy position.
points: Doubling rooks (here on d1 and d2) wins control of the file — a single rook can be challenged.
The goal is to invade: a rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns and confines the king.
Contest open files early; once the enemy doubles, you may never get in.

practice.prompt: Click the square where White's rooks want to invade.
practice.explain: The 7th rank: a rook on d7 attacks pawns and cramps the king.

name: Piece activity
mnemonic: Improve your worst piece.
summary: A piece is only as good as the squares it controls. Active pieces win games even without extra material.
points: Material is equal, but White's rook on the 7th and centralised knight dominate Black's undeveloped rook and knight.
Ask every move: which piece is doing least? Move that one.
Trade your bad pieces; keep your good ones.

practice.prompt: Click White's most active piece.
practice.explain: The rook on c7 attacks a7 and f7 and ties Black down.

name: King safety
mnemonic: Pawns in front of your king are walls — every pawn move is a brick removed.
summary: Castle early, keep the pawn shield intact, and don't open lines towards your own king.
points: ...h6 and ...g5 gained time against the bishop but tore holes on f5 and h5 next to Black's king.
White's knight heads for f5 via h4; the queen can follow to h5.
Count attackers vs defenders around the king; if the attackers outnumber defenders, a sacrifice may work.

practice.prompt: Click the hole next to Black's king that White's knight is heading for.
practice.explain: ...g5 gave up control of f5; Nh4–f5 lands there.

name: Space advantage
mnemonic: More space, more room to manoeuvre — but more ground to defend.
summary: Pawns further up the board give your pieces more squares behind them and restrict the opponent's pieces.
points: White's pawns on c4, d5 and e4 claim the queenside and centre; Black claims the kingside with ...f5.
The side with less space should trade pieces — cramped positions suffocate when crowded.
The side with more space should avoid trades and prepare a pawn break to open lines.

practice.prompt: Click White's most advanced pawn — the spearhead of the space advantage.
practice.explain: The d5-pawn cramps Black's pieces and supports c4–c5.

name: Good vs bad bishop
mnemonic: A bishop is bad when its own pawns stand on its colour.
summary: A bishop that is blocked by its own pawns is 'bad'; one whose pawns are on the other colour is 'good'.
points: Black's pawns on d5 and e6 sit on light squares, so the c8-bishop is hemmed in — a classic French bad bishop.
White's f1-bishop is good: his pawns on d4 and e5 are on dark squares, leaving its diagonals open.
Plans: trade your bad bishop (...b6 and ...Ba6), or put your pawns on the other colour.

practice.prompt: Click Black's bad bishop.
practice.explain: The c8-bishop is hemmed in by its own pawns on d5 and e6.

name: Initiative
mnemonic: Make threats; force your opponent to react instead of plan.
summary: The player who makes the threats dictates the game. The initiative can be worth a pawn or more.
points: Black is a pawn down, but every move came with a threat: ...Na5 hit the bishop, ...h6 the knight, ...e4 the knight again.
While White retreats, Black develops; soon ...Bc5/...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Qc7 follow with an attack.
To keep the initiative, keep creating threats — one quiet move can hand it back.

practice.prompt: Click the pawn that is making Black's threat.
practice.explain: ...e4 hits the f3-knight; White must react instead of developing.

name: Opening principles
mnemonic: Centre, develop, castle — and don't move a piece twice without a reason.
summary: Most games below 1500 are decided by opening principles, not memorised lines.
points: Fight for the centre (e4, d4, e5, d5) with pawns and pieces.
Develop knights and bishops before moving the queen or rooks.
Castle early — usually within the first ten moves.
Connect your rooks; then start a plan.

practice.prompt: Click the square where White's c1-bishop develops with a pin.
practice.explain: Bg5 develops with a pin on the f6-knight.

name: Isolated queen's pawn
mnemonic: Active pieces with it, blockade and endgame against it.
summary: A d-pawn with no neighbours: weak in the endgame, but it gives space and open files for an attack.
points: Black's d5-pawn has no c- or e-pawn to protect it.
White blockades on d4 and piles up on d5; trading pieces helps White.
Black wants active pieces, a kingside attack, or the ...d4 break.

practice.prompt: Click Black's isolated pawn.
practice.explain: d5 has no pawns on the c- or e-file to support it.

name: Minority attack
mnemonic: Two pawns attack three to leave one weak.
summary: In the Carlsbad structure White pushes the b-pawn (two pawns vs three) to create a weak black c-pawn.
points: b4–b5 and bxc6 leave Black with a backward c-pawn or an isolated d-pawn.
The rooks then attack the weakness on the half-open c-file.
Black's counterplay is on the kingside (...Ne4, ...Ng6, ...f5).

practice.prompt: Click the pawn White's minority attack is aiming at.
practice.explain: b5xc6 turns c6 into a weak, backward pawn.

name: Prophylaxis
mnemonic: Ask what your opponent wants — then stop it.
summary: A prophylactic move prevents the opponent's plan before it happens.
points: h3 stops ...Bg4, which would pin the f3-knight and pressure d4.
After h3, White can play d4 without the centre being undermined.
Before each move ask: 'What is my opponent's best idea?'

practice.prompt: Click the square h3 takes away from Black.
practice.explain: ...Bg4 (or ...Ng4) is no longer possible.

name: The bishop pair
mnemonic: Two bishops cover every colour — open the position for them.
summary: Two bishops together control both colour complexes and are usually worth more than bishop + knight in open positions.
points: White's bishops rake both long diagonals; Black's knight has no outposts.
Open the position with pawn breaks to give the bishops scope.
The side with the knight wants a closed position and fixed pawns.

practice.prompt: Click Black's minor piece that is weaker than a bishop in this open position.
practice.explain: The f6-knight has no stable outpost; in open positions bishops outrange it.

name: Opposite-coloured bishops
mnemonic: Drawish in the endgame, deadly in an attack.
summary: Bishops of different colours can never fight each other: in attack the attacker effectively has an extra piece; in a pure endgame they are very drawish.
points: White's light bishop hits f7; Black's dark bishop can never defend that square.
With queens on, attack the squares the enemy bishop can't cover.
In a pawn endgame with opposite bishops, even two extra pawns may not win.

practice.prompt: Click the target White's bishop attacks that Black's bishop can never defend.
practice.explain: f7 is a light square; Black's bishop is dark-squared.

name: Pawn breaks
mnemonic: Know your break before the position closes.
summary: A pawn break challenges the opponent's chain to open lines for your pieces. In closed positions it is the whole plan.
points: In the King's Indian Black breaks with ...f5, White with c5.
Prepare the break: support the square and get pieces behind it.
Once a break is played, open lines appear — make sure your pieces are ready.

practice.prompt: Click the square where Black's key pawn break lands.
practice.explain: ...f5 attacks e4 and opens the f-file for Black's rook.

name: Pawn majority
mnemonic: Push the candidate first — the pawn with no opponent in front.
summary: Where you have more pawns than the opponent, you can create a passed pawn. Lead with the pawn that has no opposing pawn on its file.
points: White has 3 pawns vs 2 on the queenside; Black has 4 vs 3 in the centre/kingside.
The c-pawn is the 'candidate': no black pawn stands on its file.
A queenside majority far from the kings is especially strong in endgames.

practice.prompt: Click the pawn White should push first to make a passed pawn.
practice.explain: The c-pawn has no opposing pawn in front of it — it becomes the passer.

name: Trade when ahead
mnemonic: Ahead in material? Trade pieces, not pawns.
summary: Every trade makes an extra piece count for more. When ahead, offer exchanges; when behind, avoid them.
points: White is a knight up. After the rooks come off, the win is trivial.
Rd8+ offers the trade with tempo.
When behind, keep pieces on and create complications.

practice.prompt: Click the square where White offers the rook trade.
practice.explain: Rd8+ forces ...Rxd8 or a passive retreat; either way White's extra knight dominates.

name: Blockade
mnemonic: Stop a passed pawn by sitting on the square in front of it.
summary: A passed pawn is stopped most reliably by a piece placed directly in front of it — ideally a knight, which loses no activity there.
points: The d3-knight blockades the d4-pawn and still controls c5, e5, b4 and f4.
A blockaded passed pawn often becomes a weakness.
Rooks belong behind passed pawns; knights in front of enemy ones.

practice.prompt: Click White's blockading piece.
practice.explain: The knight on d3 stops the d-pawn dead.

name: Knight vs bad bishop
mnemonic: Closed position + fixed pawns = knight's paradise.
summary: In closed positions with fixed pawns, a knight that reaches a strong square can beat a bishop blocked by its own pawns.
points: Black's light-squared bishop is hemmed in by its own pawns on a6 and b5 and has no good diagonal.
White's knight travels d2–b3–a5–c6 to an outpost no pawn can attack.
Plan the knight's route several moves ahead — in closed positions knights have time.

practice.prompt: Click the outpost White's knight is heading for.
practice.explain: From c6 the knight hits a7/b8/d8/e7 and can never be chased by a pawn.
